### Cancer is a scary word for pet parents.  

Roughly 12 million dogs and cats are diagnosed with cancer each year. Statistics show cancer is a top cause of death in both cats and dogs. Odds are that pet owners will be faced with this disease at some point in their pet’s life.

The good news is advances in therapy over the last 40 years have helped give pets a fighting chance to enjoy a high quality, longer life.

UQ Gatton trials cancer drug that could cure dogs with terminal tumours (https://www.couriermail.com.au/news/toowoomba/uq-gatton-launches-trial-to-treat-dogs-with-incurable-and-inoperable-cancers/news-story/5e9606a8b1b2d225f7fa2a9ce870f488)
【turn1096news18】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; The University of Queensland (UQ) Gatton has launched a clinical trial testing a new cancer drug, Enzistat, developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune. Led by Professor Rachel Allavena, the trial explores Enzistat’s potential to help dogs with inoperable or terminal tumors. Early data indicate the drug may extend survival and reduce side effects in canine cancer patients. The study is now seeking 60 participating dogs: 30 with inoperable tumours and 30 in palliative care. The goal is to shrink tumors for potential surgery or improve quality of life for terminal cases. Participants must have a cancer diagnosis and veterinary referral, and owners are required to administer the medication twice daily for six weeks and attend three visits to UQ Gatton. While the drug and necessary diagnostics are provided, all other vet costs are the owner’s responsibility. This research also holds promise for human cancer treatments. Interested parties can contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au for more information.
UQ Gatton trials cancer drug that could cure dogs with terminal tumours
Date: Mon Feb  9 01:00:00 2026 UTC

UQ Gatton Professor Rachel Allavena said the drug Enzistat developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune has the potential to treat cancers in dogs and humans. "It gives dogs in southeast Queensland another option, and it's always nice to do cutting edge trials," she said. "The early data that the company has is that it's helped dogs survive longer and have less bad side effects from their cancer. "We're quite hopeful that for dogs that might not have a lot of options that it might be a useful drug in the future." UQ is looking for 30 dogs with inoperable tumours and 30 dogs in palliative care to be part of the trial. Professor Allavena said they hope the drug can shrink inoperable tumours so they could be removed surgically and give a final hope for dogs in palliative care. "They don't have hope for a cure any other way, but their owners just want to see if they can keep them to be around a little longer and see if it can make them more comfortable," she said. She said a third to a half of dogs will get cancer and it is more common than in lots of other species. Professor Allavena has been researching immune-based cancer therapies for about 15 years and she said it was really hard at times. "It's really hard when we hear about one of our patients passing away," she said. "We do also get a lot of joy from giving people hope or giving the animals options." Anyone interested in joining the trial need a cancer diagnosis and referral from their vet. People involved in the trial would need to give a tablet to their dog twice a day for six weeks and need to come to UQ Gatton three times throughout the trial. The medication and any additional blood tests, biopsies, or examinations are provided as part of the study and owners have to cover any other veterinary costs. Contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au to join the trial.

Of course the ChatGPT dog cancer vaccine spawned a startup (https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/978671/ai-cured-dog-cancer-mrna-vaccine-startup-gamgee)
【turn1096news19】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 2 months ago; Paul Conyngham, an Australian tech entrepreneur, has launched a startup named Gamgee that aims to develop personalized mRNA cancer vaccines for dogs, inspired by his own dog Rosie’s battle with cancer. He claims to have used AI tools like ChatGPT and computational genomics to craft a vaccine that led to shrinkage in Rosie's tumors. Though Gamgee focuses on pet care, its broader ambition extends to personalized treatment for various species, including humans.

Rosie’s case, which features prominently in Gamgee’s marketing, has drawn skepticism from experts who question the scientific validity of the claims, noting that Rosie received multiple treatments, making it unclear if the mRNA vaccine caused her improvement. Despite scientific uncertainties, Gamgee has received backing from Y Combinator and is preparing for clinical trials in Australia, with global recruitment underway. The company promises a simple, quick process for veterinarians and highlights promising initial results, though based on a single case.

Gamgee is collaborating with Australian universities and aims to scale its personalized medicine approach, although its foundation rests on unverified anecdotal outcomes.

Cats could help scientists better understand human cancer, study says (https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/2026/05/30/scientists-find-cancer-gene-similarities-cats-humans-study-says/)
【turn1096news20】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 4 months ago; A recent study led by Louise van der Weyden and international researchers has discovered significant genetic similarities between feline and human cancers, offering promising avenues for shared treatment advancements. Analyzing tumor samples from nearly 500 domestic cats across multiple countries, the researchers identified common mutations in about 1,000 cat genes that correspond to human cancer genes. Among the most striking parallels was the FBXW7 gene, a tumor suppressor found mutated in both feline mammary tumors and human breast cancer, associated with poor prognoses.

Published in the journal Science, the research underlines cats as effective disease models due to their genetic closeness to humans and shared living environments that expose them to similar carcinogens. The study also revealed chemotherapy drug vincristine’s effectiveness in treating feline mammary tumors, providing a potential pathway for clinical trials and the development of targeted treatments. While experts like Jaime Modiano stress that more research is needed, the findings mark a significant step toward dual-species cancer therapy, benefiting both feline and human patients.

Inspired by his determination to save his rescue dog Rosie from cancer using artificial intelligence, Conyngham developed a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine after chemotherapy failed. The treatment, supported by scientists at the University of NSW and the University of Queensland, extended Rosie's life by two years. Although Rosie was eventually euthanized due to an aggressive tumor recurrence, her legacy will continue through Gamgee’s upcoming clinical trials on 30–50 dogs with cancer. These trials aim to replicate Rosie's personalized vaccine treatment and will be free for pet owners. Influential figures such as OpenAI founder Sam Altman and Elon Musk have praised the initiative, with other notable seed investors joining the venture. Gamgee represents a promising intersection of AI and biotechnology, with aspirations to eventually extend its success to human treatments.

Pan-tumor CAnine cuTaneous Cancer Histology (CATCH) dataset (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11446)
【turn1096academia23】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 4.7 years ago; 
Title: Pan-tumor CAnine cuTaneous Cancer Histology (CATCH) dataset
Authors: Frauke Wilm, Marco Fragoso, Christian Marzahl, Jingna Qiu, Chloé Puget, Laura Diehl, Christof A. Bertram, Robert Klopfleisch, Andreas Maier, Katharina Breininger, Marc Aubreville
Date: Thu Jan 27 11:16:26 2022

Due to morphological similarities, the differentiation of histologic sections of cutaneous tumors into individual subtypes can be challenging. Recently, deep learning-based approaches have proven their potential for supporting pathologists in this regard. However, many of these supervised algorithms require a large amount of annotated data for robust development. We present a publicly available dataset of 350 whole slide images of seven different canine cutaneous tumors complemented by 12,424 polygon annotations for 13 histologic classes, including seven cutaneous tumor subtypes. In inter-rater experiments, we show a high consistency of the provided labels, especially for tumor annotations. We further validate the dataset by training a deep neural network for the task of tissue segmentation and tumor subtype classification. We achieve a class-averaged Jaccard coefficient of 0.7047, and 0.9044 for tumor in particular. For classification, we achieve a slide-level accuracy of 0.9857. Since canine cutaneous tumors possess various histologic homologies to human tumors the added value of this dataset is not limited to veterinary pathology but extends to more general fields of application.

Comparative oncology
Comparative oncology integrates the study of oncology in non-human animals into more general studies of cancer biology and therapy. The field encompasses naturally seen cancers in veterinary patients and the extremely low rates of cancers seen in large mammals such as elephants and whales.
## Mammalian cancers

Species that are treated in the veterinary clinic, including dogs, cats, horses and ferrets, present human-relevant cancers.
### Canines

Of these, the dog has the greatest number of incidents. One in four dogs older than 2 dies of cancer, a rate that has increased, which may in part be explained by reductions in other causes of death. Canine cancer shares features with human cancer, including histology, tumor genetics, molecular targets, biological behavior and therapeutic response. Canine histologies include osteosarcoma, melanoma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, leukemia, prostate, breast and lung cancer, head and neck cancer, soft tissue sarcomas and bladder cancer.

A Common Plant Virus Is an Unlikely Ally in the War on Cancer (https://www.wired.com/story/a-common-plant-virus-is-an-unlikely-ally-in-the-war-on-cancer)
【turn1096news25】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 6.0 years ago; Researchers are exploring the use of the cowpea mosaic virus (CPMV), a common plant virus, as an innovative cancer immunotherapy treatment. At Dartmouth College, veterinary oncologist Jack Hoopes has seen promising results when injecting virus-like particles derived from CPMV directly into tumors in dogs with oral cancer, leading to unexpectedly long remissions. The virus doesn't replicate in mammals but effectively stimulates the immune system to attack cancer cells. Collaborating with nanoengineer Nicole Steinmetz and immunologist Steve Fiering, the team discovered that CPMV triggers a strong immune response, reducing tumor growth and recurrence in mice and dogs.

Unlike traditional oncolytic viruses that directly kill cancer cells, CPMV works by mobilizing an immune response without replication, offering a safer and potentially more effective alternative. They've begun developing human trials and testing innovative delivery systems, including a virus-releasing implant for ovarian cancer. Despite challenges such as understanding why CPMV is so effective and navigating regulatory hurdles, early findings suggest plant virus-based cancer therapies could enhance existing treatments. Researchers have founded a company, Mosaic IE, to bring this therapy to human clinical trials, aiming to improve patient outcomes through combination therapies.

Veterinary oncology
Cancer diagnosis and treatment in animals
Mast cell tumor on muzzle of dog

Veterinary oncology is a subspecialty of veterinary medicine that deals with cancer diagnosis and treatment in animals. Cancer is a major cause of death in pet animals. In one study, 45% of the dogs that reached 10 years of age or older died of cancer.

Skin tumors are the most frequently diagnosed type of tumor in domestic animals for two reasons: 1. constant exposure of animal skin to the sun and external environment, 2. skin tumors are easy to see because they are on the outside of the animal.
## History

Specialised veterinary oncology training became available in the 21st century.
## Treatment

The most effective method of treating cancer in animals is surgery. Surgery may involve a marginal excision, where just the capsule is excised; wide excision, where a wider area surrounding the capsule (typically 2–3cm) is excised; or radical excision, where the entire compartment is excised, often taking the form of an amputation.

CVac
Immunotherapeutic agent that was 1st developed in Australia
CVac (short for Cancer Vaccine), is an immunotherapeutic agent that was 1st developed in Australia.

CVac was developed by the biotechnology company Prima BioMed (Nasdaq: PBMD) through to Phase II clinical studies between 2001 and 2015. After inconclusive clinical data in ovarian cancer 2013 and 2014, Prima announced in February 2015 that it had ceased recruiting into CVAc clinical studies and was seeking commercial partners for the product.
## Treatment method

CVac is an ex vivo dendritic cell priming technology involving MFP, or mannan fusion protein, where a fusion protein of MUC1 and Glutathione S-transferase is coupled to oxidized polymannose. The dendritic cells are the orchestrators of the immune system. 'Priming' dendritic cells involves exposing those cells to disease antigens in order to get the immune system to properly recognise the antigen and mount an appropriate response.

【turn1096news29】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; A groundbreaking study published in *Science* finds that cats share significant genetic similarities with humans concerning cancer-causing mutations, positioning them as valuable partners in cancer research. Researchers discovered that the most frequently mutated gene, TP53, appears in 33% of feline cancers and 34% of human tumors. The findings point to critical parallels between feline and human oncogenes, highlighting cats as effective models for comparative cancer studies. Cats also share similar living environments and disease mechanisms with humans, bolstering support for the “one health” concept that links human, animal, and environmental health. The study found particularly strong correlations in breast cancer and squamous cell carcinoma between the species. Researchers, including those from Cornell University's College of Veterinary Medicine and the Wellcome Sanger Institute, emphasize the potential for precision feline oncology, which could ultimately advance cancer treatment in both animals and humans.

Systematic Review of Methods and Prognostic Value of Mitotic Activity. Part 1: Feline Tumors (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01403)
【turn1096academia31】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 3.5 years ago; 
Title: Systematic Review of Methods and Prognostic Value of Mitotic Activity. Part 1: Feline Tumors
Authors: Christof A. Bertram, Taryn A. Donovan, Alexander Bartel
Date: Tue May  2 13:22:12 2023

Increased proliferation is a key driver of tumorigenesis, and quantification of mitotic activity is a standard task for prognostication. The goal of this systematic review is scholarly analysis of all available references on mitotic activity in feline tumors, and to provide an overview of the measuring methods and prognostic value. A systematic literature search in PubMed and Scopus and a manual search in Google Scholar was conducted. All articles on feline tumors that correlated mitotic activity with patient outcome were identified. Data analysis revealed that of the eligible 42 articles, the mitotic count (MC, mitotic figures per tumor area) was evaluated in 39 instances and the mitotic index (MI, mitotic figures per tumor cells) in three instances. The risk of bias was considered high for most studies (26/42, 62%) based on small study populations, insufficient details of the MC/MI methods, and lack of statistical measures for diagnostic accuracy or effect on outcome. The MC/MI methods varied markedly between studies. A significant association of the MC with survival was determined in 21/29 (72%) studies, while one study found an inverse effect. There were three tumor types with at least four studies and a prognostic association was found in 5/6 studies on mast cell tumors, 5/5 on mammary tumors and 3/4 on soft tissue sarcomas. The MI was shown to correlate with survival by two research groups, however a comparison to the MC was not conducted. An updated systematic review will be needed with of new literature for different tumor types.

Dataset on Bi- and Multi-Nucleated Tumor Cells in Canine Cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors (https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01445)
【turn1096academia32】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 5.8 years ago; 
Title: Dataset on Bi- and Multi-Nucleated Tumor Cells in Canine Cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors
Authors: Christof A. Bertram, Taryn A. Donovan, Marco Tecilla, Florian Bartenschlager, Marco Fragoso, Frauke Wilm, Christian Marzahl, Katharina Breininger, Andreas Maier, Robert Klopfleisch, Marc Aubreville
Date: Tue Jan  5 10:35:41 2021

Tumor cells with two nuclei (binucleated cells, BiNC) or more nuclei (multinucleated cells, MuNC) indicate an increased amount of cellular genetic material which is thought to facilitate oncogenesis, tumor progression and treatment resistance. In canine cutaneous mast cell tumors (ccMCT), binucleation and multinucleation are parameters used in cytologic and histologic grading schemes (respectively) which correlate with poor patient outcome. For this study, we created the first open source data-set with 19,983 annotations of BiNC and 1,416 annotations of MuNC in 32 histological whole slide images of ccMCT. Labels were created by a pathologist and an algorithmic-aided labeling approach with expert review of each generated candidate. A state-of-the-art deep learning-based model yielded an $F_1$ score of 0.675 for BiNC and 0.623 for MuNC on 11 test whole slide images. In regions of interest ($2.37 mm^2$) extracted from these test images, 6 pathologists had an object detection performance between 0.270 - 0.526 for BiNC and 0.316 - 0.622 for MuNC, while our model archived an $F_1$ score of 0.667 for BiNC and 0.685 for MuNC. This open dataset can facilitate development of automated image analysis for this task and may thereby help to promote standardization of this facet of histologic tumor prognostication.

Title: Computational diagnosis and risk evaluation for canine lymphoma
Authors: E. M. Mirkes, I. Alexandrakis, K. Slater, R. Tuli, A. N. Gorban
Date: Tue May 21 20:03:30 2013

The canine lymphoma blood test detects the levels of two biomarkers, the acute phase proteins (C-Reactive Protein and Haptoglobin). This test can be used for diagnostics, for screening, and for remission monitoring as well. We analyze clinical data, test various machine learning methods and select the best approach to these problems. Three family of methods, decision trees, kNN (including advanced and adaptive kNN) and probability density evaluation with radial basis functions, are used for classification and risk estimation. Several pre-processing approaches were implemented and compared. The best of them are used to create the diagnostic system. For the differential diagnosis the best solution gives the sensitivity and specificity of 83.5% and 77%, respectively (using three input features, CRP, Haptoglobin and standard clinical symptom). For the screening task, the decision tree method provides the best result, with sensitivity and specificity of 81.4% and >99%, respectively (using the same input features). If the clinical symptoms (Lymphadenopathy) are considered as unknown then a decision tree with CRP and Hapt only provides sensitivity 69% and specificity 83.5%. The lymphoma risk evaluation problem is formulated and solved. The best models are selected as the system for computational lymphoma diagnosis and evaluation the risk of lymphoma as well. These methods are implemented into a special web-accessed software and are applied to problem of monitoring dogs with lymphoma after treatment. It detects recurrence of lymphoma up to two months prior to the appearance of clinical signs. The risk map visualisation provides a friendly tool for explanatory data analysis.
